newsitem.title: PERU: Rescuers trawl Pacific for Peru air crash bodies.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers trawl Pacific for Peru air crash bodies.

text.p: Peruvian rescue workers trawled the icy waters of the Pacific for a third day on Friday, looking for bodies and debris from the Boeing 757-200 airliner that crashed on Wednesday killing all 70 on board.
By mid-morning on Friday, only 14 bodies had been recovered by the navy-led team of helicopters, frigates and private boats, which has been scouring the crash site since dawn on Wednesday.

The other 56 corpses were believed still trapped 180 yards (metres) below the surface in the trunk of the plane. The Peruvian government was waiting for help from the United States to reach the main wreckage on the ocean floor.
Rescuers fished out sneakers, clothes, briefcases, and personal documents floating on the waters.
Bitter at the slow progress in the rescue operations, relatives of the victims, who came from 11 countries, also said they would appeal to foreign governments for assistance.
Aeroperu, the local airline that owned the plane, said it would fly relatives over the crash site later on Friday.

A U.S.-led investigative team started preliminary work to determine why computers aboard the plane "went crazy," leaving pilot Eric Schreiber without instruments as he struggled to guide his jet to Lima airport, according to Transport Minister Elsa Carrera de Escalante.

Carrera said the inquiry would centre on computer failures aboard the jet based on recordings of a dramatic, 29-minute dialogue between the pilot and Lima air control, which showed Schreiber did not know whether he was flying over land or sea before he plunged into the ocean.

Boeing's spokesman in Seattle, Russ Young, told Reuters it was "too early to even guess" what happened to the plane which, according to President Alberto Fujimori, had only been in service for three months.
At the morgue in Lima's port of Callao only eight bodies were identified. The other corpses were too disfigured for positive identification, officials said.
Relatives who identified bodies were asked to provide clothes for their dead family members to be buried in.

Wednesday's crash, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to local Faucett airline crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa.
Since 1967, a total of 601 people have been killed in air crashes in Peru. Aeroperu, privatised in 1993 and 100 percent owned by Aeromexico, was operating flights normally on Thursday.
